items.passage: Programs that pay landowners to conserve forests are widely used, but their effectiveness has rarely been rigorously evaluated. After randomly selecting 60 of 121 villages in western Uganda to receive a program that paid forest owners to leave their trees standing, ______ tree cover fell by 4.2 percent in participating villages, compared with 9.1 percent in the others.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: economist Seema Jayachandran and her colleagues used satellite imagery to show that
satellite imagery enabled economist Seema Jayachandran and her colleagues to show that
economist Seema Jayachandran and her colleagues’ analysis of satellite imagery showed that
it was shown by economist Seema Jayachandran and her colleagues through satellite imagery that
items.explanation: The opening phrase “After randomly selecting 60 of 121 villages ... to receive a program” describes whoever did the selecting, so the subject of the main clause must be the researchers. Only choice A makes “economist Seema Jayachandran and her colleagues” that subject; in B the subject is “satellite imagery,” in C it is “analysis,” and in D it is the empty “it.”

B.why_wrong: The subject is “satellite imagery,” so the sentence says the imagery selected the villages.

C.why_wrong: The researchers appear only in a possessive; the subject is “analysis,” which could not have selected any villages.

D.why_wrong: The subject is the empty “it,” so nothing in the main clause can do the selecting and the opening phrase dangles.

sources.what: PES program in Uganda: randomized trial in 121 villages, 60 received payments to forest-owning households for conserving forest; tree cover measured with high-resolution satellite imagery declined 4.2% in treatment vs 9.1% in control villages
abstract of the Science paper (Jayachandran, de Laat, Lambin, Stanton, Audy, Thomas 2017)
program located in western Uganda
described as the first rigorous evaluation of a promising and popular type of intervention

items.rewrite: New subject (Uganda payments-for-ecosystem-services trial, Jayachandran 2017) replacing Vera Rubin; denser two-sentence setup; option set uses imagery-as-subject, possessive agent and expletive instead of the 2.17 pattern.

items.passage: Stanford University researcher Mireille Kamariza helped develop an alternative to auramine O, a decades-old stain that is still the standard means of detecting tuberculosis bacteria in sputum but that cannot reveal whether the bacteria it marks are alive. By mimicking trehalose, a sugar that mycobacteria build into their waxy outer membrane, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: live mycobacteria incorporate the probe DMN-Tre into that membrane, where it begins to glow within minutes.
the incorporation of the probe DMN-Tre into that membrane by live mycobacteria makes the probe glow within minutes.
the probe DMN-Tre is incorporated into that membrane by live mycobacteria and begins to glow within minutes.
DMN-Tre’s incorporation into that membrane by live mycobacteria causes the probe to glow within minutes.
items.explanation: The opening phrase “By mimicking trehalose” must describe the subject of the main clause, and only the probe imitates the sugar. Choice C makes “the probe DMN-Tre” the subject, using the passive so that the bacteria still appear as the agents of incorporation. In A the subject is “live mycobacteria,” and in B and D it is “incorporation,” none of which mimics trehalose.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “live mycobacteria,” so the sentence says the bacteria mimic trehalose; the active voice makes it tempting, but the modifier dangles.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the incorporation,” an action that cannot mimic a sugar.

D.why_wrong: The probe appears only in the possessive “DMN-Tre’s”; the subject is “incorporation,” so the modifier dangles.

sources.what: DMN-Tre: trehalose analog conjugated to a solvatochromic dye, >700-fold fluorescence increase once metabolically incorporated into the mycomembrane; labeling detected within minutes; absent in heat-killed bacteria; reduced by TB drugs unlike auramine; tested on TB-positive sputum
abstract of Kamariza et al. 2018, Science Translational Medicine
existing stains have been around for decades; auramine O is the standard labeling method and binds acids in cell walls; existing methods cannot tell live from dead cells
graduate student Mireille Kamariza and chemistry professor Carolyn Bertozzi of Stanford developed the DMN-Tre test

fixes: “Chemist Mireille Kamariza and colleagues have developed” changed to “Stanford University researcher Mireille Kamariza helped develop”: her affiliation on the paper is the Department of Biology, so “chemist” was not supported, and “and colleagues” was a stock opener; source added

items.rewrite: New subject (DMN-Tre tuberculosis probe, Kamariza 2018) replacing the Eastgate Centre; passive key with an active-voice wrong-subject trap, nominalised and possessive distractors.

items.passage: The four facade niches of New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art stood empty from the facade’s completion in 1902 until 2019, when Kenyan American artist Wangechi Mutu filled them. Cast in bronze and adorned with polished disks recalling the lip plates traditionally worn by some African women, ______ allude to caryatids, the sculpted women who serve as columns in Greek and West African architecture.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Mutu created four seated figures that
the four seated figures Mutu created
there are four seated figures by Mutu that
the museum displayed four seated figures that
items.explanation: The opening phrase “Cast in bronze and adorned with polished disks recalling the lip plates traditionally worn by some African women” describes sculptures, so the subject that follows the comma must name them. Choice B makes “the four seated figures Mutu created” the subject, with “figures” as its head noun. In A the subject is Mutu, in C it is the empty “there,” and in D it is the museum, none of which was cast in bronze.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Mutu,” so the sentence says the artist herself was cast in bronze and adorned with polished disks.

C.why_wrong: The subject is the empty “there,” so the opening phrase has no noun to describe; the figures sit inside the clause instead.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the museum,” so the sentence says the museum was cast in bronze and adorned with disks.

sources.what: Kenyan-American artist Wangechi Mutu; four bronze sculptures of seated African women in coiled garments with polished discs referencing the lip plates worn by women in some African tribes; they reference the West African and Greek tradition of caryatids; first artworks in the Fifth Avenue facade niches since the building’s completion in 1902

first time in 117 years that sculptures occupy the empty niches of the Met’s exterior; disks reminiscent of lip plates traditionally worn; column-like caryatids sculpted from marble in Greece and wood in West Africa
The NewOnes, will free Us: four bronze sculptures, The Seated I to IV (2019); facade completed in 1902 with four niches that have long lain empty; first-ever installation on the museum’s exterior
Met press release: Kenyan-American artist; niches always intended for sculpture but long empty; on view from September 9, 2019

items.notes: Earlier subjects of this cell: Nellie Bly (replaced as a duplicate of rhetorical_synthesis.NARR.hard), Gertrude Ederle (recognised by judges as an official item) and Toyin Ojih Odutola’s A Countervailing Theory (shared subject with official boundaries item 83c9c503). Mutu, the Met and caryatids appear in no official item of any skill (cb_api grep).

fixes: replaced the subject (Toyin Ojih Odutola, shared with official 83c9c503) with Wangechi Mutu’s 2019 Met facade sculptures; passage, options, explanation, distractors and sources rewritten; 64 words (model 2.19: 45, official medium max 66); independent blind solve B

items.rewrite: New subject (Wangechi Mutu, The NewOnes, will free Us, the Met’s first Facade Commission, 2019) replacing Toyin Ojih Odutola; key is a noun phrase with a reduced relative (“the four seated figures Mutu created”), distractors are the artist as subject, an expletive “there are” and the museum as subject.

items.passage: Seismologists ordinarily image the oceanic crust with air guns towed behind ships, but such surveys require special permitting because of their potential to harm marine life; in 2021, geophysicists Václav Kuna and John Nábělek demonstrated an alternative source of seismic waves. Recorded by ocean-bottom seismometers in the northeast Pacific, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Kuna and Nábělek found echoes in fin whale songs that let them estimate the thickness of sediment and basalt layers beneath the seafloor.
the sediment and basalt layers beneath the seafloor had their thickness estimated by Kuna and Nábělek from echoes in fin whale songs.
the estimation by Kuna and Nábělek of the thickness of sediment and basalt layers beneath the seafloor relied on echoes in fin whale songs.
fin whale songs contained echoes that let Kuna and Nábělek estimate the thickness of sediment and basalt layers beneath the seafloor.
items.explanation: Only something that was recorded can follow “Recorded by ocean-bottom seismometers in the northeast Pacific.” Choice D makes “fin whale songs” the subject, and the songs are what the seismometers recorded. In A the subject is the researchers, in B it is the rock layers, and in C it is “the estimation,” none of which was recorded.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Kuna and Nábělek,” so the sentence says the researchers were recorded by seismometers.

B.recipe: passive leaving the wrong noun as subject
B.why_wrong: The subject is “the sediment and basalt layers”; the layers were measured, not recorded.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the estimation,” a process that seismometers could not record.

sources.what: fin whale songs recorded at ocean-bottom seismometers in the northeast Pacific contain signals reflected and refracted from crustal interfaces; used to constrain thickness and velocity of oceanic sediment and basaltic basement; complement to air-gun surveys
abstract of Kuna and Nábělek 2021, Science
air-gun mapping requires special permitting because of potential harm to marine life, including whales

items.notes: Cost and marine-protected-area bans for air guns appear only in secondary coverage, so the passage keeps the permitting point the OPB article states.

fixes: unsupported claim that air-gun surveys are expensive and prohibited in marine protected areas (the cited OPB article says neither) replaced with the sourced point that they require special permitting because of their potential to harm marine life; “an alternative” sharpened to “an alternative source of seismic waves,” since the authors present whale songs as a complement to air guns

items.rewrite: New subject (fin whale songs as seismic source, Kuna and Nábělek 2021) replacing the Coupé speech-rate study; key no longer begins with a study attribution, all options share the same facts.

items.passage: Geochemical measurements had indicated that in some marine sediments, electric currents couple the oxidation of sulfide in deeper, oxygen-free layers to oxygen consumption at the surface. A team at Denmark’s Aarhus University identified the conductors in 2012. Containing strings that run along their length, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the currents are carried across centimeter-wide zones of sediment by long, filamentous bacteria.
long, filamentous bacteria carry the currents across centimeter-wide zones of sediment.
it is long, filamentous bacteria that carry the currents across centimeter-wide zones of sediment.
the transport of the currents across centimeter-wide zones of sediment is performed by long, filamentous bacteria.
items.explanation: The phrase “Containing strings that run along their length” describes something long and physical, so it must attach to the bacteria. Choice B puts “long, filamentous bacteria” first after the comma. In A the subject is “the currents,” in C it is the empty “it,” and in D it is “the transport,” none of which contains strings.

A.recipe: passive leaving the wrong noun as subject
A.why_wrong: The subject is “the currents,” so the sentence says the currents contain strings.

C.why_wrong: The subject is the empty “it” of the cleft, so the opening phrase dangles.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the transport,” an action that cannot contain strings.

sources.what: oxygen consumption in marine sediments coupled to sulphide oxidation in deeper, oxygen-free layers by electric currents across centimetre-wide zones; native conductors are long filamentous bacteria containing strings along their length
abstract of Pfeffer et al. 2012, Nature
Aarhus University team (Lars Peter Nielsen, Christian Pfeffer)

fixes: the “...; in 2012, a team ...” sentence split in two: the same semicolon frame opened R3_past_participle.hard

items.replaced: Physarum slime mold maze study (duplicate of words_in_context.B4.easy)
items.rewrite: New subject (cable bacteria, Aarhus 2012) replacing the dung beetle study; key is a clean active clause with no tacked-on study attribution.

items.passage: A chart of East and Southeast Asia drawn in the early 1600s, ______ lay largely forgotten for centuries until 2008, when historian Robert Batchelor recognized that its faint lines traced Chinese merchant shipping routes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: English scholar John Selden’s collection brought the Selden Map to Oxford’s Bodleian Library in 1659, but it
Oxford’s Bodleian Library received the Selden Map in 1659 with the collection of English scholar John Selden, but it
it was in 1659 that the Selden Map reached Oxford’s Bodleian Library with the collection of English scholar John Selden, and it
the Selden Map, which reached Oxford’s Bodleian Library in 1659 with the collection of English scholar John Selden,
items.explanation: The opening noun phrase “A chart of East and Southeast Asia drawn in the early 1600s” renames the subject of the sentence, so the subject must be the map. Choice D begins with “the Selden Map” and keeps the details about Selden in a relative clause. In A the subject is Selden’s collection, in B it is the library, and in C it is the empty “it,” none of which is a chart.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “collection,” so the sentence calls Selden’s collection a seventeenth-century chart.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “Oxford’s Bodleian Library,” so the library is described as a chart of Asia.

C.why_wrong: The subject is the empty “it,” so the opening phrase renames nothing.

sources.what: Selden Map: early 17th-century map (after 1606, before 1624) of East and Southeast Asia; mentioned in Selden's 1653 will; part of the Bodleian's collections from 1659; largely forgotten since the 18th century; Robert Batchelor rediscovered it in 2008 and recognized its shipping routes
Batchelor noticed in 2008 that the fine lines marked 17th-century Chinese shipping trade routes

items.rewrite: New subject (Selden Map, Batchelor 2008) replacing A. E. Douglass; the appositive now renames a thing and the option set no longer mirrors the Behrensmeyer item.

items.passage: In Recollections of Things to Come (1963), Mexican writer Elena Garro portrays Ixtepec, a fictional southern town under military occupation during the Cristero War, the Catholic insurrection against Mexico’s anticlerical government in the late 1920s. At once the novel’s setting and its narrator, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Ixtepec recounts in the first person its residents’ suffering under the despotic General Francisco Rosas.
its residents’ suffering under the despotic General Francisco Rosas is recounted by Ixtepec in the first person.
Garro has Ixtepec recount in the first person its residents’ suffering under the despotic General Francisco Rosas.
the first-person account of its residents’ suffering under the despotic General Francisco Rosas comes from Ixtepec.
items.explanation: The opening phrase “At once the novel’s setting and its narrator” renames the subject of the main clause, and the only thing that is both setting and narrator is the town. Choice A makes “Ixtepec” the subject. In B the subject is “suffering,” in C it is the author, and in D it is “account,” none of which is the novel’s setting.

B.recipe: passive leaving the wrong noun as subject
B.why_wrong: The subject is “its residents’ suffering,” so the sentence calls the suffering the novel’s setting and narrator.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “Garro,” so the author is described as the novel’s setting and narrator.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the first-person account,” which is not the novel’s setting; Ixtepec is left in a prepositional phrase.

sources.what: Los recuerdos del porvenir (1963), translated as Recollections of Things to Come; town narrates; Ixtepec; Cristero War; Villaurrutia Prize
the I-narrator is the town itself; Ixtepec in southern Mexico occupied by the army under the despotic General Francisco Rosas during the Cristero War
Cristero War 1926 to 1929: Catholic uprising against the government's enforcement of anticlerical laws

fixes: opening “Mexican writer Elena Garro’s 1963 novel Recollections of Things to Come is set in ...” rebuilt: it kept the “[nationality] author X’s [year] novel [title]” skeleton of official 3.7 (Chraïbi), the judges’ named tell for this item

items.rewrite: New subject (Elena Garro, town-narrated novel) replacing Natsume Sōseki; passage-final full-clause options with passive, author-as-subject and nominalised distractors instead of the 3.7 frame.

items.passage: Discovered in 2016 by the Pan-STARRS survey telescope in Hawaii, the asteroid Kamoʻoalewa is a quasi-satellite of Earth: although it orbits the Sun, it remains near our planet. Astronomer Benjamin Sharkey reported in 2021 that ______ reflects sunlight much like space-weathered lunar silicates, suggesting a possible origin as a fragment of the Moon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the subject of the verb “reflects” and refers to the asteroid Kamoʻoalewa, a single object. The singular pronoun “it” matches both the antecedent and the singular verb. “They,” “these,” and “both” are plural and do not fit.

A.why_wrong: “They” is plural, but the antecedent is the single asteroid and the verb “reflects” is singular.

B.why_wrong: “These” is plural and has no plural antecedent; it also clashes with the singular verb “reflects.”

D.why_wrong: “Both” needs two things, but the passage describes one asteroid.

sources.what: Kamoʻoalewa discovered 27 April 2016 by Pan-STARRS 1 at Haleakalā, Hawaii; quasi-satellite of Earth
Sharkey et al. 2021: reddened reflectance spectrum best matched by lunar-like silicates, implying space weathering and possible lunar material
published version, Communications Earth & Environment 2, 231 (2021)

items.notes: The lunar-origin interpretation is presented as the 2021 team's suggestion; a 2026 JWST study has questioned it, so the passage keeps it hedged.

fixes: “astronomer Benjamin Sharkey and colleagues” trimmed to the lead author (stock “and colleagues” opener)

items.rewrite: New subject (asteroid Kamoʻoalewa, Sharkey 2021) replacing El Anatsui; plain two-sentence setup with no plural-heavy lead-in.

items.passage: Ancient Mesoamericans were making rubber by at least 1600 BCE, combining latex from the Castilla elastica tree with juice from morning glory vines. Researchers Michael Tarkanian and Dorothy Hosler found that the proportions determined how the rubber performed. Equal volumes of latex and juice made ______ most elastic, ideal for balls, whereas extra latex produced a more wear-resistant material for sandals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the rubber” in the previous sentence: mixing the ingredients in equal volumes made the rubber most elastic. “Rubber” is singular, so “it” is correct. The plural nouns nearby (“volumes,” “latex and juice”) may tempt “them” or “those,” but it is the rubber, not the ingredients, that becomes elastic.

B.why_wrong: “Them” is plural and would point to the ingredients, but the thing made elastic is the singular “rubber.”

C.why_wrong: “These” is a plural demonstrative with no plural antecedent that could become elastic.

D.why_wrong: “One” introduces an unspecified item instead of referring back to the rubber already named.

sources.what: Mesoamericans made rubber by at least 1600 BC from Castilla elastica latex and Ipomoea alba (morning glory) juice; 1:1 ratio maximizes elasticity for balls, about 25% juice maximizes wear resistance for sandal soles
abstract and MIT affiliations of Tarkanian and Hosler 2011, Latin American Antiquity

fixes: option set it / them / those / one was the exact set of official 2.15; “those” replaced with “these” (still wrong for the same reason)

items.rewrite: New subject (Mesoamerican rubber recipes, Tarkanian and Hosler 2011) replacing seahorses; bare-pronoun options with no copied “we” distractor; plural ingredients as the attractor.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner vs contraction
items.passage: Beginning in 2008, Chamorro poet Craig Santos Perez has published a series of books about his home island of Guam. Each is titled from unincorporated territory followed by a Chamorro word in brackets, such as [saina] or [guma’]. Weaving together childhood memories, oral histories, and colonial records, the books trace Guam’s past and ______ present status as a US territory.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank describes the present status of Guam, a single island, so the singular possessive determiner “its” is needed. “Their” is plural and would point to the books, which are not a US territory. “It’s” and “they’re” are contractions (“it is,” “they are”), not possessives.

A.why_wrong: “Their” is plural and would refer to the books, but the status as a US territory belongs to Guam.

B.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is,” which makes no sense before “present status.”

C.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are” and is also plural.

sources.what: series from unincorporated territory: [hacha] 2008, [saina] 2010, [guma’] 2014, [lukao] 2017, [åmot] 2023; about his home island of Guam and Chamoru culture
[saina] collages primary texts and oral histories of colonial domination with stories of his childhood on Guam
interconnected volumes 2008 to 2023, Chamorro language woven into the English text

fixes: “Since 2008, ... has published” changed to “Beginning in 2008”: “Since 2005, ... has transformed” opened R2_finite_main.hard

items.rewrite: New subject (Craig Santos Perez, from unincorporated territory) replacing Bashō; the plural antecedent is natural (a series of books) and the key is now “its” for Guam.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner vs contraction
items.passage: Brittle stars, relatives of sea stars, have no eyes, though some species have photoreceptors scattered across their skin. Biologist Lauren Sumner-Rooney showed in 2020 that the Caribbean brittle star Ophiocoma wendtii orients toward dark objects only by day, when pigment cells expanding across ______ arms apparently screen those photoreceptors, narrowing the angle from which each can receive light.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The arms belong to Ophiocoma wendtii, the single brittle star that is the subject of the clause (“orients”), so the singular possessive “its” is correct. The plural nouns around the blank (“brittle stars,” “dark objects,” “pigment cells”) tempt “their,” but none of them owns the arms in this clause. “They’re” and “it’s” are contractions, not possessives.

A.why_wrong: “Their” is plural, but the arms belong to the single brittle star Ophiocoma wendtii; the nearby plural “pigment cells” is only an attractor.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is,” which cannot come before “arms.”

sources.what: O. wendtii orients to visual stimuli, but the response disappears when chromatophores are contracted; chromatophores screen photoreceptors and narrow angular aperture (Sumner-Rooney et al. 2020, Current Biology)
abstract of the 2020 paper
photoreceptor networks across the bodies of Ophiocoma species; brittle stars lack eyes
red brittle star studied on Caribbean coral reefs; daytime vision stops at night as chromatophores contract; moved toward a black bar on a white wall

fixes: antecedent “the Caribbean species Ophiocoma wendtii” changed to “the Caribbean brittle star Ophiocoma wendtii”: “species” is a collective-looking noun, so a student could defend “their” (the members’ arms); first sentence now says “photoreceptors,” so “those photoreceptors” has a clear referent; “Lauren Sumner-Rooney’s team reported that” changed to “Lauren Sumner-Rooney showed that” (repeated “reported that” lead-in)

items.rewrite: New subject (brittle star Ophiocoma wendtii, Sumner-Rooney 2020) replacing the Forbidden City; plural attractors on both sides of the pronoun.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid
items.passage: Haitian painter Hector Hyppolite, a third-generation Vodou priest, initially painted on cardboard using chicken feathers because he owned no brushes. After moving to Port-au-Prince in 1946, he received free materials from the Centre d’Art and completed hundreds of paintings before his death in 1948. Scenes of Vodou ritual dominate the ______ from those years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The works belong to one painter, Hyppolite, so the possessor takes a singular possessive, “painter’s.” The works themselves are a plain plural (the hundreds of paintings just mentioned) and need no apostrophe, so the noun is “works.” Only choice D has both forms right.

A.why_wrong: “Painters” lacks the apostrophe that shows the works belong to the painter.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Work’s” is not possessive here; the plural “works” takes no apostrophe.

C.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
C.why_wrong: “Painters’” refers to several painters, but the passage names one, and “work’s” wrongly adds an apostrophe.

sources.what: third-generation Vodou priest; painted on cardboard with chicken feathers because he owned no brushes; brought to Port-au-Prince in 1946; Centre d'Art provided free materials; 250 to 600 paintings in last three years; died 1948; typically depicted Vodou scenes
MoMA collection entry for Hyppolite (moved to the capital at about 52)

items.notes: The count of paintings is given only as “hundreds” because sources estimate 250 to 600.

fixes: blank sentence “Many of the ______ depict Vodou scenes” rebuilt as “Scenes of Vodou ritual dominate the ______ from those years”: it repeated the “many of the [profession]’s [plural]” frame of official 1.16; explanation updated

items.rewrite: New subject (Hector Hyppolite) replacing Maria Sibylla Merian; two-slot grid with the key not the longest option.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid
items.passage: Sociologist Jacqueline Adams’s 2013 book Art Against Dictatorship examines arpilleras, cloth pictures that women in Santiago’s poorest neighborhoods made during Augusto Pinochet’s rule (1973–1990) to depict unemployment, poverty, and repression. Human rights groups smuggled the pictures out of Chile and sold them abroad, where they earned money for their makers and publicized the ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The abuses belong to one regime, Pinochet’s, so the possessor needs a singular possessive, “regime’s.” The abuses themselves are simply plural and take no apostrophe. Choice A is the only option with both forms correct.

B.why_wrong: “Regimes” is a plain plural; it needs an apostrophe to show possession, and the passage refers to one regime.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Abuse’s” is wrong because “abuses” is a plain plural, not a possessive.

D.why_wrong: “Regimes’” refers to several regimes, but the passage describes only Pinochet’s.

sources.what: arpilleras: cloth appliqué pictures made by poor women in Santiago's shantytowns under Pinochet depicting unemployment, poverty and repression; smuggled out by human rights organizations, raising international awareness of the regime's abuses and earning income; Jacqueline Adams, Art Against Dictatorship (University of Texas Press, 2013)

items.rewrite: New subject (Chilean arpilleras, Jacqueline Adams 2013) replacing Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru; options now end the sentence with its period, not the Paine “author’s political writings” shape.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid (plural possessive)
items.passage: From 2005 to 2015, a network of more than 1,100 agricultural researchers, working with extension agents, helped about 20.9 million Chinese smallholder farmers adopt locally tailored practices for growing maize, rice, and wheat. Across the participating ______ average yields rose by about 11 percent while nitrogen fertilizer use fell by roughly 15 to 18 percent.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The fields belong to the participating farmers, and about 20.9 million of them took part, so the possessor must be the plural possessive “farmers’.” The fields themselves are a plain plural, “fields,” with no apostrophe. Only choice C has both forms right.

A.why_wrong: “Farmer’s” refers to a single farmer, but the passage describes 20.9 million participants.

B.why_wrong: “Farmers” lacks the possessive apostrophe, and “fields’” adds one to a noun that owns nothing.

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural

sources.what: 2005 to 2015: about 20.9 million farmers in 452 counties adopted enhanced practices for maize, rice and wheat; yields rose 10.8 to 11.5%; nitrogen application fell 14.7 to 18.1%; network of 1,152 researchers with extension agents (Cui, Zhang et al. 2018)
abstract of the Nature paper

items.notes: Campaign leaders are not named: the paper describes a core network of 1,152 researchers working with extension agents, and no source says Cui and Zhang led it.

fixes: “a campaign led by agricultural scientists Zhenling Cui and Fusuo Zhang” generalised to the network of more than 1,100 researchers the paper describes (Cui is first author, but the sources do not say the two led the campaign); “roughly 20.9 million Chinese smallholders” now “about 20.9 million Chinese smallholder farmers,” which also plants the plural possessor cue; explanation updated

items.rewrite: New subject (China smallholder campaign, Cui and Zhang 2018) replacing Gaia; fuller setup and a possessor-plus-noun grid instead of the 3.24 relative-clause shape.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two nouns
items.passage: Because coffee, cashew, and avocado trees remain productive for decades, their cultivation requires long-term planning. A 2022 study by researchers at the Zurich University of Applied Sciences, based on 14 global circulation models and soil parameters, projects that by 2050, ______ prospects will diverge: negative climate impacts are expected to dominate in every major coffee-producing region, whereas the global area suitable for cashew should expand.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The colon makes clear that coffee and cashew each have separate prospects (one negative, one expanding), so this is individual possession and both nouns need an apostrophe: “coffee’s and cashew’s.” Putting the apostrophe only on the second noun would signal shared prospects, which cannot “diverge.”

A.why_wrong: “Coffees and cashews” are plain plurals with no possessive, so nothing owns the prospects.

C.why_wrong: “Coffee and cashew’s” treats the prospects as shared by both crops, but the passage describes two separate, diverging outlooks.

D.recipe: missing apostrophe on the second possessor
D.why_wrong: “Cashews” lacks the apostrophe, so cashew is not shown as owning its prospects.
